questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
try:
    print("a", end="")
except ValueError:
    print("b", end="")
else:
    print("c", end="")
finally:
    print("d", end="")
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
try:
    print("a", end="")
except ValueError:
    print("b", end="")
else:
    print("c", end="")
finally:
    print("d", end="")
```
questions.explanation_es: Sin excepción, el `except` se salta y corre el `else`; el `finally` se ejecuta siempre. Poner en el `else` lo que solo tiene sentido si el `try` fue bien evita capturar por accidente errores de ese código.
questions.explanation_en: With no exception, the `except` is skipped and the `else` runs; the `finally` always executes. Putting into `else` what only makes sense if the `try` succeeded avoids accidentally catching errors raised by that code.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §8.3 (handling exceptions)

questions.question_es:
¿Qué devuelve la siguiente función?

```python
def f():
    try:
        return 1
    finally:
        return 2

print(f())
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following function return?

```python
def f():
    try:
        return 1
    finally:
        return 2

print(f())
```
questions.explanation_es: El `finally` se ejecuta antes de que la función salga de verdad, y su `return` sustituye al anterior. Por eso devolver desde un `finally` se considera mala práctica: puede descartar en silencio un valor o incluso una excepción en curso.
questions.explanation_en: The `finally` runs before the function truly exits, and its `return` supersedes the earlier one. That is why returning from a `finally` is considered bad practice: it can silently discard a value, or even an exception in flight.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: The try statement

questions.question_es: ¿Qué problema tiene capturar con `except Exception:` un bloque muy grande?
questions.question_en: What is the problem with wrapping a very large block in `except Exception:`?
options_es: Oculta errores de programación que convenía ver y complica localizar la causa
Es más lento que capturar una excepción concreta
options_en: It hides programming errors worth seeing and makes the cause harder to locate
It is slower than catching a specific exception
It does not catch network errors
It forces you to add a `finally`
questions.explanation_es: Un `NameError` por una errata quedaría atrapado junto al error que sí esperabas, y el programa seguiría como si nada. Lo recomendable es capturar lo concreto y acotar el `try` a la línea que puede fallar.
questions.explanation_en: A `NameError` from a typo would be caught alongside the error you actually expected, and the program would carry on as if nothing happened. The recommendation is to catch specifics and keep the `try` around the line that can actually fail.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §8.3 / PEP 8 (programming recommendations)

questions.explanation_es: Los `except` se prueban en orden y gana el primero compatible. Como `ZeroDivisionError` hereda de `ArithmeticError`, el bloque más específico queda inalcanzable: siempre va primero el más concreto.
questions.explanation_en: The `except` clauses are tried in order and the first compatible one wins. Since `ZeroDivisionError` inherits from `ArithmeticError`, the more specific block becomes unreachable: the narrowest one always goes first.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Exceptions (exception hierarchy)

questions.question_es: El bloque `finally` se ejecuta aunque el `try` contenga un `return`.
questions.question_en: The `finally` block runs even when the `try` contains a `return`.
questions.explanation_es: Se ejecuta siempre: con `return`, con excepción y con `break`. Por eso es el sitio para liberar recursos, aunque un `with` suele expresarlo mejor.
questions.explanation_en: It always runs: on `return`, on exception and on `break`. That is why it is the place to release resources, though a `with` usually expresses it better.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §8.6 (defining clean-up actions)

questions.question_es: Completa la palabra clave que asocia la excepción capturada a un nombre: `except ValueError ___ e:`
questions.question_en: Complete the keyword binding the caught exception to a name: `except ValueError ___ e:`
questions.explanation_es: `as e` da acceso al objeto de la excepción para leer su mensaje o sus atributos. En Python 3, `e` deja de existir al salir del bloque `except`.
questions.explanation_en: `as e` gives access to the exception object so you can read its message or attributes. In Python 3, `e` ceases to exist once the `except` block ends.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §8.3 (handling exceptions)

questions.question_es: ¿Por qué `except:` a secas es peor que `except Exception:`?
questions.question_en: Why is a bare `except:` worse than `except Exception:`?
options_es: Porque también atrapa `KeyboardInterrupt` y `SystemExit`, impidiendo cerrar el programa
options_en: Because it also catches `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`, preventing the program from being stopped
Because it does not allow `as e`
Because it is forbidden since Python 3
questions.explanation_es: Esas dos heredan de `BaseException`, no de `Exception`, precisamente para que no las capture quien atrapa errores normales. Con `except:` dentro de un bucle, ni Ctrl+C detiene el programa.
questions.explanation_en: Those two inherit from `BaseException` rather than `Exception`, precisely so that code catching ordinary errors does not swallow them. With a bare `except:` inside a loop, not even Ctrl+C stops the program.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Exceptions (BaseException) / PEP 8

questions.explanation_es: En la vuelta 1 el `continue` sale del `try`, pero el `finally` se ejecuta igual antes de saltar: por eso hay dos «f» seguidas. El `finally` no se salta nunca, tampoco con `continue` o `break`.
questions.explanation_en: On pass 1 the `continue` leaves the `try`, but the `finally` still runs before jumping: hence two consecutive 'f's. The `finally` is never skipped, not even by `continue` or `break`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: The try statement

questions.question_es: ¿Qué excepción lanza abrir un fichero que no existe con `open("no.txt")`?
questions.question_en: Which exception does opening a non-existent file with `open("no.txt")` raise?
questions.explanation_es: Desde Python 3.3, `IOError` es solo un alias de `OSError`, y `FileNotFoundError` es la subclase concreta. Capturar `OSError` también funciona, pero atrapa además permisos y disco lleno.
questions.explanation_en: Since Python 3.3, `IOError` is merely an alias of `OSError`, and `FileNotFoundError` is the specific subclass. Catching `OSError` also works, but additionally swallows permissions and disk-full errors.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Exceptions: OSError / PEP 3151

questions.question_es: ¿Qué excepción lanza `int("abc")`, y por qué no es un `TypeError`?
questions.question_en: Which exception does `int("abc")` raise, and why is it not a `TypeError`?
options_es: `ValueError`: el tipo es correcto (string), pero el contenido no sirve
`TypeError`: un string no puede convertirse a entero
`SyntaxError`: el texto no es un número válido
options_en: `ValueError`: the type is right (a string), but the content is unusable
`TypeError`: a string cannot be converted to an integer
`SyntaxError`: the text is not a valid number
questions.explanation_es: La distinción es útil: `TypeError` significa «tipo equivocado» —como `int([])`— y `ValueError` significa «tipo correcto, valor inadecuado». Saber cuál esperar hace el `except` mucho más preciso.
questions.explanation_en: The distinction is useful: `TypeError` means 'wrong type' — as in `int([])` — while `ValueError` means 'right type, unsuitable value'. Knowing which to expect makes the `except` far more precise.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Exceptions: ValueError / TypeError

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
try:
    {"a": 1}["b"]
except LookupError:
    print("lookup")
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
try:
    {"a": 1}["b"]
except LookupError:
    print("lookup")
```
questions.explanation_es: `KeyError` e `IndexError` heredan de `LookupError`, así que capturarla atrapa ambas. Es útil cuando da igual si el fallo vino de un diccionario o de una lista.
questions.explanation_en: `KeyError` and `IndexError` both inherit from `LookupError`, so catching it traps either. That is handy when it does not matter whether the failure came from a dictionary or a list.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Exceptions: LookupError

questions.question_es: ¿Qué excepción lanza usar una variable que nunca se definió?
questions.question_en: Which exception does using a variable that was never defined raise?
questions.explanation_es: `NameError` es para nombres que no existen en ningún ámbito. Su pariente `UnboundLocalError` aparece cuando el nombre sí es local pero se lee antes de asignarlo.
questions.explanation_en: `NameError` is for names that exist in no scope at all. Its relative `UnboundLocalError` shows up when the name is local but is read before being assigned.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Exceptions: NameError

questions.question_es: `except (ValueError, TypeError) as e:` captura ambas excepciones con un solo bloque.
questions.question_en: `except (ValueError, TypeError) as e:` catches both exceptions in a single block.
questions.explanation_es: La tupla agrupa varios tipos cuando el manejo es idéntico. Los paréntesis son obligatorios: sin ellos la sintaxis cambia de significado y el segundo nombre se interpretaría como el destino de `as`.
questions.explanation_en: The tuple groups several types when the handling is identical. The parentheses are required: without them the syntax changes meaning and the second name would be read as the `as` target.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §8.3 (handling exceptions)

questions.question_es: Completa la excepción que lanza `"texto".foo()` al invocar un método inexistente: `___Error`
questions.question_en: Complete the exception raised by `"text".foo()` when calling a non-existent method: `___Error`
questions.explanation_es: `AttributeError` cubre atributos y métodos que el objeto no tiene. Es la que aparece al llamar un método sobre `None`, uno de los errores más frecuentes en Python.
questions.explanation_en: `AttributeError` covers attributes and methods the object does not have. It is the one that shows up when calling a method on `None`, among the most frequent errors in Python.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Exceptions: AttributeError

questions.question_es: ¿Cuál es la raíz de la jerarquía de excepciones en Python?
questions.question_en: What is the root of Python's exception hierarchy?
questions.explanation_es: De `BaseException` cuelgan `Exception` —de donde salen casi todos los errores— y aparte `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` y `GeneratorExit`. Las excepciones propias deben heredar de `Exception`, nunca de `BaseException`.
questions.explanation_en: From `BaseException` hang `Exception` — the ancestor of nearly every error — and separately `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit`. Custom exceptions should inherit from `Exception`, never from `BaseException`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Exceptions (exception hierarchy)

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
try:
    None.algo
except AttributeError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
try:
    None.something
except AttributeError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)
```
questions.explanation_es: `type(e).__name__` da el nombre de la clase de la excepción, útil para registrar sin depender del mensaje. El error completo sería `'NoneType' object has no attribute 'algo'`, el clásico de olvidar comprobar un `None`.
questions.explanation_en: `type(e).__name__` gives the exception class name, useful for logging without depending on the message. The full error would be `'NoneType' object has no attribute 'something'`, the classic result of forgetting to check for `None`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Exceptions / Built-in Functions: type()

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
try:
    raise ValueError("mal dato")
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
try:
    raise ValueError("bad data")
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
```
questions.explanation_es: Imprimir la excepción muestra solo su mensaje, no el nombre de la clase. Para incluir el tipo hay que pedirlo: `f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"`.
questions.explanation_en: Printing the exception shows its message only, not the class name. To include the type you have to ask for it: `f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §8.4 (raising exceptions)

questions.question_es: ¿De qué debería heredar una excepción propia como `SaldoInsuficienteError`?
questions.question_en: What should a custom exception such as `InsufficientFundsError` inherit from?
options_es: De `Exception`, o de una excepción base propia de la aplicación
De nada: basta con definir la clase
options_en: From `Exception`, or from the application's own base exception
From nothing: defining the class is enough
questions.explanation_es: Heredar de `Exception` la hace capturable por quien atrape errores normales. Definir además una base propia —`class MiAppError(Exception)`— permite a quien usa la librería capturar todos sus errores de una vez.
questions.explanation_en: Inheriting from `Exception` makes it catchable by anyone trapping ordinary errors. Defining an application base as well — `class MyAppError(Exception)` — lets library users catch all of its errors in one clause.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §8.5 (user-defined exceptions)

questions.explanation_es: `raise` sin argumentos vuelve a lanzar la excepción en curso conservando su traza original. Es el patrón para registrar un error y dejarlo subir, sin perder de dónde vino.
questions.explanation_en: A bare `raise` re-raises the exception currently being handled, preserving its original traceback. It is the pattern for logging an error and letting it propagate, without losing where it came from.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §8.4 (raising exceptions)

questions.question_es: ¿Qué aporta `raise MiError("...") from e` frente a `raise MiError("...")`?
questions.question_en: What does `raise MyError("...") from e` add over `raise MyError("...")`?
options_es: Encadena las excepciones: la traza muestra la causa original
Evita que la nueva excepción se propague
Convierte `e` en el tipo de la nueva excepción
Suprime por completo el mensaje anterior
options_en: It chains the exceptions: the traceback shows the original cause
It stops the new exception from propagating
It converts `e` into the new exception's type
It suppresses the earlier message entirely
questions.explanation_es: La traza muestra «The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception», que es lo que permite traducir un error técnico a uno de dominio sin perder el rastro. Con `from None` se oculta la causa a propósito.
questions.explanation_en: The traceback shows 'The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception', which is what lets you translate a technical error into a domain one without losing the trail. With `from None` the cause is hidden deliberately.
questions.source: PEP 3134 — Exception Chaining and Embedded Tracebacks

questions.question_es: Una excepción personalizada puede recibir atributos propios en su `__init__`.
questions.question_en: A custom exception can take its own attributes in `__init__`.
questions.explanation_es: Es una clase normal: puede guardar el saldo disponible, el campo que falló o un código de error. Quien la capture lee esos datos sin tener que analizar el mensaje de texto.
questions.explanation_en: It is an ordinary class: it can carry the available balance, the field that failed, or an error code. Whoever catches it reads those values instead of parsing the message text.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §8.5 (user-defined exceptions)

questions.question_es: Completa la sentencia que lanza una excepción con un mensaje: `___ ValueError("mal")`
questions.question_en: Complete the statement raising an exception with a message: `___ ValueError("bad")`
questions.explanation_es: `raise` interrumpe el flujo y propaga la excepción hacia arriba hasta que alguien la capture. Si nadie lo hace, el programa termina mostrando la traza.
questions.explanation_en: `raise` interrupts the flow and propagates the exception upwards until something catches it. If nothing does, the program ends printing the traceback.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §8.4 (raising exceptions)

questions.question_es: ¿Cuándo conviene lanzar una excepción en vez de devolver `None` ante un error?
questions.question_en: When is raising an exception preferable to returning `None` on error?
options_es: Cuando el fallo no debe pasar desapercibido y seguir sería incorrecto
Siempre, `None` nunca es una respuesta válida
Solo dentro de librerías, nunca en aplicaciones
options_en: When the failure must not go unnoticed and continuing would be wrong
Always, `None` is never a valid answer
Only inside libraries, never in applications
questions.explanation_es: Devolver `None` obliga a quien llama a comprobarlo, y si lo olvida el error aparece más tarde y más lejos, como un `AttributeError` confuso. La excepción falla en el punto exacto del problema.
questions.explanation_en: Returning `None` forces the caller to check, and if they forget, the error surfaces later and further away, as a confusing `AttributeError`. An exception fails at the exact point of the problem.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §8 / PEP 20 (errors should never pass silently)

questions.explanation_es: Un objeto es instancia de su clase y de todas sus ancestras. Por eso `except Exception` captura las excepciones propias, y por eso el orden de los `except` va de lo específico a lo general.
questions.explanation_en: An object is an instance of its class and of every ancestor. That is why `except Exception` catches custom exceptions, and why `except` clauses run from specific to general.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Functions: isinstance() / Tutorial §8.5

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
class C:
    def __enter__(self):
        print("in", end="")
        return self
    def __exit__(self, *a):
        print("out", end="")

with C():
    print("-", end="")
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
class C:
    def __enter__(self):
        print("in", end="")
        return self
    def __exit__(self, *a):
        print("out", end="")

with C():
    print("-", end="")
```
questions.explanation_es: `__enter__` corre al entrar y `__exit__` al salir, envolviendo el cuerpo. Ese par es todo lo que hace falta para que una clase funcione con `with`.
questions.explanation_en: `__enter__` runs on entry and `__exit__` on exit, wrapping the body. That pair is all a class needs to work with `with`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: With Statement Context Managers

questions.question_es: ¿Qué ventaja tiene `with open("f") as fh:` sobre `fh = open("f")`?
questions.question_en: What advantage does `with open("f") as fh:` have over `fh = open("f")`?
options_es: Cierra el fichero al salir del bloque, incluso si se lanza una excepción
Permite abrir varios ficheros a la vez
options_en: It closes the file on leaving the block, even if an exception is raised
It allows opening several files at once
questions.explanation_es: Sin `with` hay que acordarse de `close()` y colocarlo en un `finally` para que también corra al fallar. El `with` lo garantiza y deja el código más corto.
questions.explanation_en: Without `with` you must remember `close()` and place it in a `finally` so it also runs on failure. The `with` guarantees it and leaves the code shorter.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §7.2.1 (reading and writing files)

questions.explanation_es: `__exit__` corre aunque haya excepción, y al devolver `False` deja que siga propagándose. Devolver `True` la silenciaría, algo que casi nunca conviene: escondería errores reales.
questions.explanation_en: `__exit__` runs even on exception, and returning `False` lets it keep propagating. Returning `True` would swallow it, which is almost never advisable: it would hide real errors.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: With Statement Context Managers

questions.question_es: ¿Qué permite el decorador `@contextlib.contextmanager`?
questions.question_en: What does the `@contextlib.contextmanager` decorator allow?
options_es: Crear un context manager con una función generadora y un `yield`
Convertir cualquier función en un `with` automáticamente
Capturar todas las excepciones del bloque
options_en: Creating a context manager from a generator function with a `yield`
Turning any function into a `with` automatically
Catching every exception in the block
questions.explanation_es: Lo de antes del `yield` es el `__enter__` y lo de después el `__exit__`, normalmente dentro de un `try`/`finally`. Ahorra escribir una clase entera para un recurso sencillo.
questions.explanation_en: Whatever comes before the `yield` is the `__enter__` and what follows is the `__exit__`, usually inside a `try`/`finally`. It saves writing a whole class for a simple resource.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — contextlib.contextmanager

questions.question_es: `with` puede gestionar varios recursos en una sola sentencia, separados por comas.
questions.question_en: `with` can manage several resources in a single statement, separated by commas.
questions.explanation_es: `with open("a") as fa, open("b") as fb:` abre ambos y los cierra en orden inverso. Si el segundo falla al abrirse, el primero se cierra igualmente.
questions.explanation_en: `with open("a") as fa, open("b") as fb:` opens both and closes them in reverse order. If the second fails to open, the first is still closed.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: The with statement

questions.question_es: Completa el método especial que se ejecuta al salir de un bloque `with`: `def ___(self, exc_type, exc, tb):`
questions.question_en: Complete the special method that runs when leaving a `with` block: `def ___(self, exc_type, exc, tb):`
questions.explanation_es: Recibe el tipo, el valor y la traza de la excepción, o tres `None` si todo fue bien. Esos parámetros permiten actuar distinto según haya habido error o no.
questions.explanation_en: It receives the exception's type, value and traceback, or three `None`s if all went well. Those parameters let it behave differently depending on whether an error occurred.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: With Statement Context Managers

questions.question_es: ¿Qué devuelve `__enter__` y para qué sirve ese valor?
questions.question_en: What does `__enter__` return, and what is that value for?
options_es: Lo que se asigna al nombre tras `as`; suele ser el propio objeto o el recurso
Un booleano que indica si el bloque debe ejecutarse
La excepción que se vaya a lanzar
options_en: Whatever gets bound to the name after `as`; usually the object itself or the resource
A boolean saying whether the block should run
The exception that is about to be raised
questions.explanation_es: En `with open(...) as fh`, `fh` es lo que `__enter__` devolvió. No tiene que ser el gestor: un gestor de conexiones puede devolver un cursor, por ejemplo.
questions.explanation_en: In `with open(...) as fh`, `fh` is what `__enter__` returned. It need not be the manager itself: a connection manager might return a cursor, for instance.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: With Statement Context Managers

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
from contextlib import suppress

with suppress(ZeroDivisionError):
    1 / 0
print("sigue")
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
from contextlib import suppress

with suppress(ZeroDivisionError):
    1 / 0
print("continues")
```
questions.explanation_es: `suppress` ignora las excepciones indicadas, equivalente a un `try`/`except`/`pass` pero explícito en la intención. El bloque se abandona en el punto del fallo: nada posterior dentro del `with` llega a ejecutarse.
questions.explanation_en: `suppress` ignores the listed exceptions, equivalent to `try`/`except`/`pass` but explicit about the intent. The block is abandoned at the point of failure: nothing after it inside the `with` runs.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — contextlib.suppress
